criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and neighborhood access to drinking water services in Bukavu, DRC, including piped REGIDESO network coverage, public standpipes, unimproved sources, and parallel water markets.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain = yes -> plain_criterion2_decision = include) but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (narrow = no -> decision = exclude, E03). Under the plain wording, the study explicitly discusses institutional governance challenges, historical urban planning frameworks (1927-2021 plans, SDAU, PUR), unsystematic land titling and building permits, and neighborhood land tenure insecurity. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, the study's actual analytical exposure is spatial/demographic urban sprawl, distance from the city center, steep landslide-prone topography, and insufficient treatment plant capacity. It does not examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing water service access: it analyzes neither utility tenure/documentation eligibility requirements for connections (indeed p. 16 notes that informal areas rely on individual connections along tertiary roads, while pp. 15 and 19 frame untitled plots and absent cadasters as hindering urban planning and physical pipe right-of-way), nor water-access administrative burdens (the phrase 'administrative burdens' on p. 15 refers to reasons for not obtaining plot land titles), nor tariff/disconnection rules (beyond a single passing sentence noting tenant disputes over unpaid water bills).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical mixed-methods study combining multi-temporal Landsat (1984-2024) and Pleiades GIS spatial/cost-distance analysis, a structured survey of 655 households across 67 blocks in all 14 districts of Bukavu, and semi-structured interviews with REGIDESO officials and public authorities.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple household and neighborhood water access outcomes: network connection/access rates (61% citywide; >60% in central neighborhoods vs. <20% in peripheral/informal neighborhoods; 45% to 75% across communes), weekly distribution frequency (3 to 6 days/week), reliance on standpipes (45%), unimproved sources (32.8%), and the parallel market (43.7%), and average water collection time (45 min) and distance.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (households, n = 655, and neighborhoods/communes in Bukavu), primary exposure (urban sprawl, distance from city center, and geomorphological/informal-settlement constraints), access outcomes, and mixed-methods cross-sectional/diachronic spatial study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study evaluates urban growth and access to drinking water in Bukavu from 1980 to 2024, combining diachronic Landsat image analysis, demographic and geospatial data, and household surveys.
A total of 655 households were sampled in 67 blocks for the survey. The overall sample size was calculated to ensure an absolute error slightly above 0.05 with a 95% probability.

Central neighborhoods, notably Nyawera, Labotte, Mukukwe, and Pageco, have connection rates above 60%, while peripheral neighborhoods such as Cahi, Cimpunda, Nyakaliba, Kajangu, and Ciriri have rates below 20% in several cases (Figure 4).

Procedures for issuing land titles and building permits appear to be unsystematic, and exchanges between technical services remain limited. The institutional officials interviewed pointed to the lack of an operational urban policy framework to implement the strategies announced at the national level.

Customary, administrative, and informal land tenure systems overlap, leading to situations of parallel title holdings and persistent land conflicts. These inconsistencies hinder urban planning and complicate the installation of drinking water infrastructure. Poor regular connection to the drinking water network has been recorded in areas where most households lack formal land titles.
In informal settlements, the lack of a land registry, irregular plot sizes, and complex occupancy statuses make it difficult to secure the right-of-way necessary for installing pipes.

raw_response.exposure: Urban sprawl (spatial expansion of built-up area from 1980 to 2024, distance from the city center, steep landslide-prone terrain, and informal settlement morphology) alongside general urban planning and institutional capacity constraints
raw_response.outcome: Household and neighborhood drinking water service access and connection rates, weekly distribution frequency, reliance on standpipes, unimproved sources, and the parallel market, collection distance and time, and waterborne disease occurrence
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households and neighborhoods in Bukavu, South Kivu, DRC (n = 655 surveyed households across 67 blocks in 14 districts within 3 communes, plus REGIDESO officials and municipal/technical authorities interviewed)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the active 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although the study empirically examines household drinking water access in Bukavu (n = 655 households plus GIS analysis) and discusses broad urban governance challenges, historical urban master plans, and neighborhood land tenure informality (which would satisfy the plain literal wording of Criterion 2), its actual exposure is physical and demographic urban sprawl, distance from the city center, geomorphological hazards, and REGIDESO production/maintenance deficits. It does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household water service access (such as tenure/documentation eligibility requirements for utility connection, administrative burdens in water applications, tariff/cost-recovery rules, or regulatory structure).
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods cross-sectional household survey, semi-structured key-informant interviews, and diachronic remote-sensing/GIS spatial analysis
